strings.LAO_Postcolonial_Backwater_desc:
Modern Lao history has been one of tragedy, submission, and underdevelopment. From the time of the Three Kingdoms to Operation Issara, Laos has long been subjected to treatment as little more than a borderland by the greater powers surrounding it, with little change since the late nineteenth century.

Weak administrative power, near-universal illiteracy, overbearing corruption, and miserable infrastructure are only a few of the myriad of issues Laos now faces after centuries of neglect. Subsistence farming remains the largest industry in Laos, and modern urban industries struggle to emerge. As such, Lao leaders have deferred to Japanese wealth in an attempt to develop the country, but only time will tell the efficacy of this strategy.
strings.LAO_Legacy_of_Operation_Issara_Unmitigat:
The Thai invasion of Laos, termed “Operation Issara” by its instigators, set back what little progress had been made in bringing Laos into the modern era. Promising bureaucrats were excised from their posts, communities were destroyed wholesale by displacement and death, major Lao roads were laid to waste, and industrial development stagnated until the conflict's end. The invasion's fallout has brought Laos into administrative, demographic, infrastructural, and economic anarchy.

Yet despite these dire issues, little has been done to address these problems seriously. Stuck in a political stasis since 1957, Vientiane has been unable to provide major relief to devastated regions or begin any meaningful reconstruction effort for the nation's ruined industry and infrastructure. As a result, most Lao live under conditions worse than those during the colonial era, apathetic about the Lao national project due to its failure to aid them or their communities in rebuilding what was lost to the Thai.
strings.LAO_King_Sisavang_Vatthana_desc:
His Majesty, Samdach Brhat Chao Mavattaha Sri Vitha Lan Xang Hom Khao Phra Rajanachakra Lao Phengdara Parama Sidha Khattiya Suriya Varman Brhat Maha Sri Savangsa Vadhana, better known as King Sisavang Vatthana, serves as the sovereign of the Kingdom of Laos.

This position guaranteed universal reverence in years past, but Prince Phetsarath Ratanavongsa's efforts to reduce the monarch's influence in politics, and King Savang Vong's forced Thai collaboration during Operation Issara made the monarchy less publicly respected. King Sisavang Vatthana's attempts to interfere in governance have only contributed to this, constantly voicing his views on government affairs and his limited power. The Lao monarchy has gone from being politically unassailable to suffering from open criticism.

Still, the monarchy's popularity remains high, despite his controversial politics, due to King Sisavang Vatthana's down-to-earth public appearances and dedication to the Buddhist faith. Thus, advocates of outright republicanism remain confined to the edges of Lao politics, fringe so long as the king can manage his public image to his political ambitions.
strings.LAO_The_Golden_Triangle_desc:
Founded by NRA General Li Mi's 93rd Division after China's defeat in the Second World War, partially upheld by unofficial Thai government backing, and consisting of the Shan states in both Burma and Thailand as well as parts of Northern Laos the Golden Triangle has become a haven for the production, transportation, and refinement of opium in Southeast Asia. Its influence rapidly expanded during the chaos of Operation Issara, as the Lao National Army — the predecessor to the Royal Lao Army — made covert links to the NRA in Burma, manufacturing and selling drugs on a previously unseen scale together.

As Operation Issara came to a close and the LNA betrayed their Thai allies, so did cooperation between the LNA and NRA come to a swift end. Almost overnight, the two armies went from partners to rivals as the NRA pulled their resources out of Laos and the LNA tried to take advantage of the confusion to put down roots in the Shan states. Even as the LNA was reconstituted into the RLA and Indochina simmered into an unsteady peace, the conflict over the Golden Triangle never ended, as the RLA and NRA continue to fight for control of the triangle.
strings.LAO_The_Royal_Lao_Army_desc:
Following the reconstitution of the Lao National Army, the Royal Lao Army was created to distance the Lao military from its recent history as a tool of oppression by Thai invaders during Operation Issara. However, it is a misnomer to label the Royal Lao Army as an army of any sort. Its soldiers are apathetic and poorly trained, its unit leaders are often nothing more than nepotistic appointees unfit to lead a platoon around a corner, and its high command is little more than lard-covered robber barons bearing the title of general.

Yet, despite its ineptitude on nearly every level as a military organization, the RLA still presents a threat to the existing democratic order of Laos. Featuring a disproportionately right-wing leadership with figures such as General Phoumi Nosavan, who only show contempt for the democratic process. The RLA's leadership is a cancer that cannot be excised without the risk of killing the patient, as any action against them could be met by a hostile military takeover, forcing the civilian government of Laos to walk the fine line of keeping the RLA far away from government affairs without incurring their wrath in full.
strings.LAO_Indochinese_Communist_Party_Insurgen:
Even as amnesty was granted to anti-colonial fighters after Lao independence in 1947, one group continued their struggle until Laos was free from all forms of imperialism. The Lao Section of the Indochinese Communist Party, propped up by its Vietnamese counterpart and a small network of supporting villages, effectively kept the fledgling Lao government from securing its northeastern border with Vietnam. Once considered a nuisance at best, the situation rapidly changed as Operation Issara began.

To defeat the Thai during Operation Issara, an unofficial agreement was struck between remnants of the legitimate Lao government and the ICP, greatly aiding in the liberation of Laos. Idolized by the Lao peasantry for their service, the ICP returned to their bases in Phongsaly and Houaphanh. Since then, the ICP “Liberated Zone” in the northeast has grown substantially, limiting the government's control there. Still, the ICP remains only a nuisance, just one far larger in scale. With neither the military nor political means to act against the Lao government, they present no existential threat to the status quo... for now.
strings.LAO_Stung_Treng_Dispute_desc:
Stung Treng Province is the newest and southernmost territory of the Lao nation. Although most of the regional populace is Lao, the area had been under Kampuchean rule between 1905 and 1949. The region's control was returned to the Lao at the beginning of Operation Issara, during which Laos was divided between the Kingdom of Luang Prabang and the Kingdom of Champassak. The latter was given the Stung Treng and Nakhon Champassak provinces, due to their closeness with the Thai government. After the operation ended in 1956, the Treaty of Taihoku restored pre-war borders between Thailand and the Indochinese neighbors. However, the treaty did not include provisions for returning the Lao-Cambodian border to its pre-war state leading to a dispute between the two nations after Laos refused to cede back occupied Stung Treng.

To resolve the dispute, the Japanese government dispatched local experts to reach a compromise. They found that Stung Treng's lowland population was almost entirely Lao, leading to the Japanese government backing the Lao position in the dispute. While this officially resolved the situation, the Kampuchean government remains seething with rage over the loss of Stung Treng Province. As a result, the northeast of Kampuchea has been rapidly militarized, revanchist sentiment within Khmer politics has significantly grown, and bilateral relations between the two nations have been utterly destroyed.
